tool.name: Gradle
tool.tagline: Flexible, incremental build tool for JVM, Android and Kotlin projects
tool.description: Gradle is the build automation tool behind most Java, Kotlin and Android projects. Build scripts written in Kotlin or Groovy declare plugins, dependencies and tasks, and Gradle runs only what changed, with caching and parallelism. Knowing it lets you build, test and publish JVM software and fix the build problems every team hits.

glossary.def: A widely used programming language for servers, business software and Android apps. Java code is compiled to bytecode that runs on the JVM.
A modern programming language that also runs on the JVM and works alongside Java; Google's preferred language for Android. Gradle's build scripts can be written in it.
The Java Virtual Machine: a program that runs Java and Kotlin bytecode, so the same compiled code works on Windows, macOS and Linux.
The Java Development Kit: the JVM plus the compiler and other tools needed to build Java programs. JDKs have version numbers such as 17 or 21.
A Java ARchive: one zip-like file holding compiled code and other files, the usual way to package a Java library or program.
The largest public repository of Java and Kotlin libraries, where most open-source JVM libraries are published and from which Gradle downloads them.
An older, widely used build tool for Java. Its repository format and POM files are the standard way JVM libraries are published, which Gradle also uses.
In Gradle, one named step of a build, such as compileJava, test or jar. Tasks depend on each other, and Gradle runs the ones needed in the right order.
Small scripts (gradlew, gradlew.bat) saved with a project that download and run the exact Gradle version the project names, so everyone builds with the same one.
A file of instructions telling Gradle how to build a project, usually build.gradle.kts (or settings.gradle.kts for the whole build).
One part of a larger Gradle build, in its own folder with its own build script, such as an app and the libraries it uses.
The way Gradle build scripts are written: Kotlin code used as a small settings language, in files ending in .kts. The older Groovy DSL does the same in Groovy.
A default that a tool assumes unless told otherwise, such as Gradle's java plugin expecting code in src/main/java, so you only configure what differs.
The JDK version Gradle uses to compile and run your code, set in the build script; Gradle can download it so every machine uses the same one.
The three-part name of a published library, group:name:version, such as org.slf4j:slf4j-api:2.0.17.
In Gradle, a named group of dependencies that says when they are needed, such as implementation, api, compileOnly or testImplementation.
The list of compiled code and libraries that the Java compiler (compile classpath) or the running JVM (runtime classpath) can see.
A library your project gets indirectly, because one of your dependencies needs it.
A library for writing automated tests: it finds your test functions, runs them and reports which passed or failed. JUnit is the standard one on the JVM.
The most widely used test framework for Java and Kotlin; version 5 is also called JUnit Jupiter.
The map Gradle builds of which tasks depend on which, used to run every needed task once, in the right order.
The part of a Gradle run in which every build script is executed to create and connect tasks, before any task does its work.
The part of a Gradle run in which the requested tasks, and the tasks they need, actually do their work.
Gradle's approach of setting things up only when needed: tasks are configured only if they will run, and values are read only when a task finally uses them.
The code a Gradle task runs when it executes, written in doFirst { } or doLast { } blocks or a @TaskAction function.
A Gradle task made from a ready-made class such as Copy, Zip, Exec or Delete, so you only fill in settings instead of writing the work yourself.
In Gradle, a placeholder for a value that is worked out later, when needed, such as a task's output file. Passing providers lets Gradle link tasks automatically.
The public online repository of community Gradle plugins, where Gradle looks for plugins by default.
Gradle skipping the recompiling of projects that use a library when only the library's private internals changed, not its public parts.
The settings block a Gradle plugin adds to the build script, such as java { } or application { }, where you configure that plugin.
A Gradle file, gradle/libs.versions.toml, listing every library and plugin with its version in one place, used from build scripts as libs.name.
A bill of materials: a published list of versions for a family of libraries that belong together. Importing it as a platform makes all those libraries use matching versions.
A Gradle build made of several subprojects listed in one settings.gradle.kts, built together and able to depend on each other.
A small plugin you write to hold the build settings your projects share (JDK version, test setup), applied by each project instead of copying the settings.
A Gradle build that includes another whole build, so you can use a local copy of a library's source code instead of its published version.
Gradle comparing a task's inputs and outputs with its previous run and skipping the task if nothing changed.
The files and settings a Gradle task reads (inputs) and the files it produces (outputs). Declaring them lets Gradle skip or reuse the task's work safely.
A store of task outputs filed under a fingerprint of their inputs, so Gradle can reuse results from earlier builds, even from other machines, instead of redoing the work.
A Gradle feature that saves the result of the configuration phase, so later builds can skip running the build scripts entirely.
An online report of one Gradle build, showing a timeline of tasks, cache hits, downloads and failures, created with --scan.
A Gradle version declaration that says more than one number, such as an allowed range plus a preferred version, or a strict limit.
In Gradle, a declared feature a library provides; two libraries providing the same capability conflict, so Gradle can catch libraries that must not be used together.
Recording the exact versions Gradle chose for every dependency in a lock file, so later builds use the same ones until you deliberately update.
In Gradle, a set of files (JARs, POM, metadata) published together as one version of a library.
Project Object Model: the XML file published next to a JVM library describing its name, version and dependencies, readable by Maven and Gradle.
A code attached to a file, made with the publisher's secret key, that lets anyone check the file really came from them and wasn't changed.
A Gradle plugin written as a compiled Kotlin or Java class, rather than as a build script, so it can be tested and published like any library.
A Gradle feature that lets a task split its work into pieces that run in parallel, safely isolated from each other.
Gradle's library for testing plugins: it runs a real Gradle build in a temporary folder and lets you check the result.
In Gradle, one of several sets of files a library offers for different uses, such as for compiling against, for running, or its source code.
A label on a Gradle variant, such as its usage or the JVM version it needs, that Gradle matches against what a project asks for to pick the right variant.
An optional part of a Gradle library, published with its own extra dependencies, which users ask for only if they need it.
In Gradle, a group of source files compiled together with their own dependencies, such as main or test.

concepts.name: What a build tool does
concepts.summary: What happens between writing Java or Kotlin code and having a program you can run, and where Gradle fits in.
concepts.why: Every later lesson assumes you know what compiling, dependencies, tests and tasks are, because those are the jobs Gradle organises.
concepts.body:
A program is a set of instructions for a computer. Programmers write them as text in a **programming language**, a precise written language computers can follow, and that text is the **source code**. Gradle is mostly used with **Java** and **Kotlin**, two popular languages for the computers behind websites, for desktop tools and for Android phone apps.

The computer can't run that text directly. A **compiler** first translates it into a lower-level form, and that step is called **compiling**. Mistakes the compiler finds stop the build with an error message.

Java and Kotlin compile to **bytecode**: instructions for the **JVM** (Java Virtual Machine), a program that runs bytecode on Windows, macOS and Linux alike. Programmers install the JVM together with the compiler and other tools as a **JDK** (Java Development Kit).

Almost no program is written from scratch. It uses **libraries**, ready-made code written by others, for jobs like reading files or sending email. A library your project needs is a **dependency**. Libraries are downloaded from a **repository**, an online store of published libraries; the biggest for Java is **Maven Central**.

Programmers also write automated tests: small extra pieces of code that run the program's code with known inputs and check the answers, so that a **bug**, a mistake that makes a program misbehave, is caught early.

Finally, the compiled code is packed into one file to run or hand out, usually a **JAR** (Java ARchive), a zip-like file of compiled code. Any file a build produces for others to use is called an **artifact**.

Doing all this by hand, in the right order, every time, is slow and error-prone. A **build tool** automates it: you describe your project once, and it downloads the dependencies, compiles, tests and packs everything up. Gradle is a build tool. It splits the work into named steps called **tasks**, such as `compileJava`, `test` and `jar`, and runs them in the right order.

You drive Gradle by typing commands in a **terminal**, the text window where you give the computer instructions by typing. `./gradlew build` means "run the build task, and every task it needs first". Gradle remembers what it did last time and skips tasks whose inputs haven't changed, which is why a second build is much faster.
concepts.code:
my-app/
  settings.gradle.kts         # names the project
  build.gradle.kts            # describes how to build it
  gradlew                     # starts Gradle (next lesson)
  src/main/java/App.java      # your source code
  src/test/java/AppTest.java  # your tests

$ ./gradlew build
> Task :compileJava           # source code -> bytecode
> Task :test                  # run the tests
> Task :jar                   # pack into build/libs/my-app.jar
BUILD SUCCESSFUL
takeaways: Source code is compiled to bytecode, which the JVM runs
Dependencies are libraries your project uses, downloaded from repositories
A build tool compiles, tests and packs up your code for you, as a series of tasks
pitfalls: Thinking Gradle itself is broken when a build fails; the error message usually points to a mistake the compiler or a test found in your code.

quiz.q: In Gradle's terms, what is a dependency?
options: A task that must run first
A library your project uses, downloaded from a repository
quiz.explain: A dependency is ready-made code from someone else that your project needs; Gradle downloads it from a repository.

quiz.q: You run ./gradlew build twice without changing anything. Why is the second run much faster?
options: Gradle skips tasks whose inputs haven't changed
The second run skips compiling by mistake
Gradle only builds every other time
quiz.explain: Gradle remembers each task's inputs and outputs and skips tasks when nothing they depend on has changed.

concepts.name: The wrapper and the command line
concepts.summary: Run builds with the Gradle wrapper (gradlew), the main built-in tasks and the most useful command-line options.
concepts.why: Every Gradle project is driven from gradlew; these commands are what you'll type every day.
concepts.body:
Different projects need different Gradle versions, and a build that works with one version can break with another. So each project carries a small **Gradle wrapper**: two **scripts**, small programs you can run, `gradlew` (macOS and Linux) and `gradlew.bat` (Windows), plus the file `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties`, which names the exact Gradle version. The first time you run `./gradlew` it downloads that version; after that it reuses it.

That way every developer, and every **CI** server (a machine that builds and tests each change automatically), builds with the same Gradle. Always run `./gradlew` rather than a `gradle` installed on your computer. Upgrade the wrapper with `./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version 9.1`.

Everyday commands:

- `./gradlew build` compiles, runs the tests and packs the result into a JAR.
- `./gradlew test` runs only the tests; `./gradlew clean` deletes the `build/` folder of earlier output.
- `./gradlew run` starts your program, when the project uses the `application` **plugin** (an add-on that teaches Gradle extra tasks).
- `./gradlew tasks` lists the available tasks; `./gradlew help --task test` explains one.
- `./gradlew projects` and `./gradlew dependencies` show how the build is put together.

Extra words starting with dashes are **command-line options** that change how Gradle runs: `-q` prints less, `--info` and `--debug` print more, `--stacktrace` shows the full details of a failure, `--offline` uses only files already downloaded, `-x test` skips a task, `--continue` keeps going after a failure, and `-p dir` builds the project in another folder.

Starting Gradle takes a few seconds, so it leaves a **daemon** running: a helper program that waits in the background so the next build starts at once. `./gradlew --stop` stops it. Its settings, such as how much **memory** it may use, live in the file `gradle.properties`.

Task names can be shortened to the capital letters of their parts: `./gradlew cT` runs `compileTestJava`, as long as no other task matches.
concepts.code:
# The wrapper's version file is saved with the project
cat gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties | grep distributionUrl
# distributionUrl=https\://services.gradle.org/distributions/gradle-9.1-bin.zip

./gradlew build                 # compile + test + package
./gradlew test --tests "com.acme.*"   # run only some tests
./gradlew build -x test         # skip the test task
./gradlew run --args="--port 8080"    # start the program (application plugin)
./gradlew tasks --all           # every task, including internal ones
./gradlew dependencies --configuration runtimeClasspath   # what the program needs to run
./gradlew clean build --offline --stacktrace
./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version 9.1   # upgrade the wrapper
./gradlew --stop                # stop the background daemon
takeaways: Use ./gradlew, never a separately installed gradle, so versions match everywhere
build = compile + test + pack into a JAR; -x skips a task
tasks, dependencies and help --task show what the build contains
A background daemon keeps later builds fast
pitfalls: Leaving the wrapper files out of the project, so teammates build with different Gradle versions.

options: Builds the project but skips the test task
quiz.explain: -x leaves the named task out of the run, along with tasks that only it needed.

quiz.q: Why should you run ./gradlew instead of a gradle command installed on your computer?
options: The wrapper uses the exact Gradle version the project names, so everyone builds the same way
quiz.explain: The wrapper downloads and uses the version written in gradle-wrapper.properties, so every developer and CI server matches.

concepts.name: Build scripts and settings
concepts.summary: Read build.gradle.kts and settings.gradle.kts: plugins, repositories, dependencies and the standard folder layout.
concepts.why: The build script is where every configuration change happens; you need to read it fluently.
concepts.body:
Gradle reads two **build scripts**, files of instructions, from the top folder of a project:

- `settings.gradle.kts` names the build (`rootProject.name = "demo"`) and, for bigger builds, lists its **subprojects**, parts that are built separately: `include("app", "lib")`. It can also say where plugins and dependencies are downloaded from.
- `build.gradle.kts` describes one project: which plugins to use, which repositories to download from, and which dependencies the code needs.

The scripts are written in the **Kotlin DSL**: Kotlin used as a small configuration language (a **domain-specific language**, a mini-language for one job), which is why the files end in `.kts`. Older projects use the Groovy DSL in `build.gradle`; the ideas are identical. You don't need to know Kotlin: a script is mostly blocks of the form `name { ... }` holding settings, and programs for writing code (a **code editor**, or a fuller **IDE**) suggest and check them as you type.

A minimal Java application:

```kotlin
plugins { id("java"); id("application") }
repositories { mavenCentral() }
dependencies { implementation("com.google.guava:guava:33.4.0-jre") }
application { mainClass = "com.acme.App" }
```

- `plugins { }` adds `java` (compiling, testing and packaging Java) and `application` (running it).
- `repositories { mavenCentral() }` downloads libraries from Maven Central.
- `implementation(...)` adds a dependency, written as `group:name:version`.
- `mainClass` names where the program starts.

Plugins come with **conventions**: sensible defaults you follow instead of configuring. The `java` plugin expects your code in `src/main/java`, tests in `src/test/java` and other files the program needs (images, settings) in `src/main/resources`. It adds the tasks `compileJava`, `test`, `jar` and `build`, and everything Gradle produces goes into the `build/` folder.

`group` and `version` give your artifacts their name and version number. The block `java { toolchain { languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(21) } }` sets the **toolchain**: Gradle compiles with JDK 21, downloading it if needed, whichever Java the computer happens to have installed. That keeps builds the same on every machine.
takeaways: settings.gradle.kts names the build and lists subprojects
build.gradle.kts applies plugins, repositories and dependencies
The java plugin sets the src/main and src/test layout and the build tasks
A toolchain fixes which JDK compiles your code

quiz.q: Where do you list the subprojects of a build?
quiz.explain: include(...) in settings.gradle.kts defines which projects make up the build.

quiz.q: With the java plugin, where does Gradle look for your main source code?
quiz.explain: By convention the java plugin compiles code from src/main/java; tests live in src/test/java.

concepts.name: Declaring dependencies
concepts.summary: Add libraries with implementation, api, compileOnly, runtimeOnly and the test configurations, and see which versions you actually got.
concepts.why: Most build changes are dependency changes; choosing the right configuration keeps builds fast and libraries tidy.
concepts.body:
You add dependencies in the `dependencies { }` block. Each is written as **coordinates**, `"group:name:version"` (for example `"org.slf4j:slf4j-api:2.0.17"`): who published it, what it's called and which version. Each line starts with a **dependency configuration**, which says when the library is needed:

- `implementation`: needed to compile and to run your code. The default choice.
- `api` (from the `java-library` plugin): when you're writing a library for others, a dependency that their projects need too, because it appears in your library's public parts. `implementation` keeps it hidden from them.
- `compileOnly`: needed only while compiling (for example helpers that generate code). `runtimeOnly`: needed only when the program runs (for example a database connector chosen when the program starts).
- `testImplementation`, `testRuntimeOnly`: the same, but only for the tests.
- `annotationProcessor`: tools such as Lombok that write extra code during compiling.

Behind these sit **classpaths**: lists of compiled code and libraries that the compiler, or the JVM running your program, can see. `implementation` puts a library on your own compile and runtime classpaths; `api` also puts it on the compile classpath of every project that uses your library.

Gradle downloads libraries from the `repositories { }` you list (`mavenCentral()`, `google()` for Android, or a company server) and keeps copies in a **cache**, `~/.gradle/caches`, so each version is downloaded only once.

Libraries have dependencies of their own, which come along automatically: these are **transitive dependencies**. When two of them ask for different versions of the same library, Gradle picks the **highest** version by default. (Maven, the older Java build tool, picks the one nearest your project instead.) See the result with `./gradlew dependencies`, or ask why a version won with `./gradlew dependencyInsight --dependency jackson-databind`.

Version ranges like `1.+` or `latest.release` make each build take whatever is newest that day, so two builds of the same code can differ; prefer exact versions. A `constraints { }` block can raise a transitive dependency to a safer version, say one that fixes a **vulnerability** (a security hole), without adding it directly. To depend on another part of the same build, write `implementation(project(":lib"))`.
takeaways: implementation hides a dependency from your library's users; api exposes it
compileOnly and runtimeOnly split compiling from running
Among conflicting transitive versions, Gradle picks the highest
dependencyInsight explains why a version was chosen
pitfalls: Using api for everything, which forces your library's internals onto every project that uses it.

quiz.q: A library you build uses Jackson only inside its own code. Which configuration should you use?
quiz.explain: implementation compiles and runs your code with Jackson while keeping it off the compile classpath of projects that use your library.

quiz.q: Two of your dependencies need library X, one at version 1.2 and one at 1.5. Which version does Gradle use by default?
quiz.explain: Gradle resolves conflicts between transitive versions to the highest one requested.

concepts.name: Running tests
concepts.summary: Run tests with Gradle's test task and JUnit 5, choose which tests run, and read the results and reports.
concepts.why: Tests run through Gradle on your machine and on CI servers; knowing its options saves hours of searching.
concepts.body:
Tests are written with a **test framework**: a library that finds your tests, runs them and reports which passed. On the JVM the standard one is **JUnit**, whose version 5 is called Jupiter. The `java` plugin adds a `test` task that compiles `src/test/java` and runs the tests in it.

To use JUnit 5, add `testImplementation("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:...")` and `testRuntimeOnly("org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher")`, then switch the task over with `tasks.test { useJUnitPlatform() }`. Newer builds can say the same with `testing { suites { ... } }` and `useJUnitJupiter()`.

Running and choosing tests:

- `./gradlew test` runs everything; `--tests "com.acme.UserTest"` or `--tests "*Integration*"` picks tests by name, where `*` matches anything.
- If nothing changed since the last run, Gradle skips the task and prints `UP-TO-DATE`; add `--rerun` (or `--rerun-tasks` for every task) to force a run.
- `--fail-fast` stops at the first failing test; `--continue` lets other tasks carry on after test failures.

Results go to a web page you can open in a browser, `build/reports/tests/test/index.html`, and to **XML** files in `build/test-results/` that CI servers read. By default Gradle prints only failures; `testLogging { events("passed", "failed"); showStandardStreams = true }` shows more, including anything the tests print.

Tests run in a separate JVM, which you can configure: `maxParallelForks` runs several test JVMs at once, and `jvmArgs`, `systemProperty("env", "ci")` and `environment(...)` pass settings in. Slow **integration tests**, which check several parts working together (often with a real database), are best kept out of the quick everyday run: mark them with tags and exclude those, or give them their own separate test task.
takeaways: useJUnitPlatform() switches the test task to JUnit 5
--tests picks tests; --rerun forces a run that would be skipped
Reports are in build/reports/tests and build/test-results
Running test JVMs side by side, and tags, speed up everyday test runs
pitfalls: Wondering why tests "didn't run": the task was UP-TO-DATE because nothing changed since last time.

quiz.q: You run ./gradlew test twice without changes. What happens the second time?
options: The test task is skipped as UP-TO-DATE
quiz.explain: Gradle skips a task whose inputs and outputs haven't changed since its last run.

concepts.name: Tasks, dependencies and lifecycle
concepts.summary: Create your own tasks, connect them with dependsOn, understand the configuration and execution phases, and use ready-made task types like Copy and Exec.
concepts.why: Your own tasks automate everything beyond compiling, and the phases explain most puzzling build behaviour.
concepts.body:
Tasks depend on each other, and together they form a **task graph**: a map of which task needs which. Running `./gradlew build` runs `build` and everything it depends on, in the right order, each task at most once.

Gradle runs in phases:

1. **Initialization**: settings script, which projects exist.
2. **Configuration phase**: every build script runs, creating tasks and connecting them. Nothing should do real work here.
3. **Execution phase**: only the requested tasks (and the tasks they need) do their work.

Create tasks with `tasks.register("name") { }`. This is **lazy configuration**: the block runs only if the task is actually needed. A task's **actions**, the work it does when it runs, go in `doLast { }` / `doFirst { }`; code outside them runs in the configuration phase on every build, a classic cause of slow builds.

**Typed tasks** come with ready-made behaviour: `Copy`, `Zip`, `Exec`, `Delete`, `JavaExec`, `Sync`. Configure them with `tasks.register<Copy>("stage") { from("docs"); into(layout.buildDirectory.dir("staging")) }`.

Connecting tasks: `dependsOn("other")` makes the other task run first, and always; `mustRunAfter` sets the order only if both run anyway; `finalizedBy` runs a clean-up task afterwards. When one task uses another's output, pass that output as a **provider**, a placeholder that hands over the value once it's ready (`from(tasks.named("jar"))`), so Gradle works out the dependency itself.

`group` and `description` make a task show up nicely in `./gradlew tasks`. Use `tasks.named("test") { }` to modify an existing task rather than creating a duplicate.
takeaways: Configuration phase runs all scripts; execution runs only requested tasks
Put work in doLast/doFirst, not in the configuration block
Typed tasks (Copy, Exec, Zip) cover common jobs
Connect tasks through outputs/providers so Gradle works out the order itself
pitfalls: Calling expensive code (shelling out, reading files) directly in a task's configuration block.

quiz.q: Where should the code that actually copies files in a custom task go?
quiz.explain: Actions run in the execution phase; code in the configuration block runs on every build, whether the task is requested or not.

concepts.name: Plugins and conventions
concepts.summary: Apply core and community plugins with the plugins block, pin versions, and understand what conventions they add.
concepts.why: Plugins are how Gradle supports Kotlin, Android, Spring Boot, code quality and publishing.
concepts.body:
Gradle itself is small; plugins add tasks, dependency configurations and conventions. Apply them in the `plugins { }` block, which must be the first block in the script:

```kotlin
plugins {
    java                                        // core plugin, no version
    id("org.springframework.boot") version "3.4.4"
    kotlin("jvm") version "2.1.20"
}
```

Core plugins (`java`, `java-library`, `application`, `maven-publish`, `jacoco`) are bundled. Community plugins, written by others, are downloaded from the **Gradle Plugin Portal** by default, or from repositories listed in `pluginManagement { repositories { } }` in `settings.gradle.kts`. Versions are pinned there or in the version catalog; in a build with subprojects, declare a plugin version once (often in the top-level script with `apply false`, meaning "know this version but don't use it here") and apply it without a version in subprojects.

What plugins give you:

- `java-library` adds `api`, and **compile avoidance**: projects that use your library are recompiled only when its public parts change.
- `application` adds `run` and `installDist`, which builds a folder with ready-to-run start scripts.
- `org.springframework.boot` (Spring Boot, a popular **framework** for web services) adds `bootRun` and `bootJar`.
- `com.android.application` turns a project into an Android app.
- `jacoco` measures test coverage (which lines your tests actually run); `checkstyle` and `spotless` check and fix code style.

Each plugin adds a **plugin extension**, a settings block for configuring it (`java { }`, `application { }`, `springBoot { }`). Prefer `plugins { }` over the legacy `apply(plugin = ...)`, where the IDE can't suggest or check the plugin's settings. You can also write your own plugins that bundle your team's settings (see Multi-project builds).
takeaways: plugins { } must come first; community plugins need a version
Core plugins are bundled; others come from the Plugin Portal or configured repositories
Each plugin adds tasks and an extension block to configure it
Pin plugin versions once per build

quiz.q: Why does id("java") not need a version while id("org.springframework.boot") does?
options: java is a core plugin bundled with Gradle; Boot is resolved from a repository
Versions are optional for all plugins
quiz.explain: Core plugins ship with Gradle itself; plugins from others are downloaded, so you must say which version.

concepts.name: Version catalogs
concepts.summary: Keep all dependency and plugin versions in one file, gradle/libs.versions.toml, and use them through libs accessors.
concepts.why: Catalogs keep versions consistent across subprojects and are the modern standard in Android and JVM builds.
concepts.body:
A **version catalog** declares dependency coordinates and versions once, in `gradle/libs.versions.toml`, a **TOML** file (a simple settings format of `[sections]` and `key = value` lines). Every build script then refers to them through the `libs` accessor: generated names such as `libs.guava` that the IDE can complete and check.

```toml
[versions]
junit = "5.11.4"
kotlin = "2.1.20"

[libraries]
guava = { module = "com.google.guava:guava", version = "33.4.0-jre" }
junit-jupiter = { module = "org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter", version.ref = "junit" }

[bundles]
testing = ["junit-jupiter"]

[plugins]
kotlin-jvm = { id = "org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm", version.ref = "kotlin" }
```

Then `implementation(libs.guava)`, `testImplementation(libs.bundles.testing)` and `plugins { alias(libs.plugins.kotlin.jvm) }`. Dashes in names become dots in accessors.

Benefits: one place to raise versions, IDE completion, no typos in long strings, and bots such as Renovate and Dependabot, which propose version upgrades automatically, understand the file. `version.ref` shares a version among related artifacts (all Kotlin or all Jackson modules), and **bundles** group libraries that are always used together.

The catalog named `libs` is picked up automatically; additional catalogs can be declared in `dependencyResolutionManagement { versionCatalogs { } }` in `settings.gradle.kts`, or published as an artifact to share between separate projects.

Catalogs don't change resolution rules: they only provide coordinates. Use a **platform**, also called a **BOM** (bill of materials: a published list of versions that belong together), with `implementation(platform(libs.spring.bom))` when transitive dependencies must use matching versions.
takeaways: gradle/libs.versions.toml holds versions, libraries, bundles and plugins
Use libs.xxx accessors; dashes become dots
version.ref shares one version across related artifacts
Catalogs provide coordinates; BOMs (platforms) make transitive versions match

quiz.q: How is a catalog library named junit-jupiter referenced in build.gradle.kts?
quiz.explain: Accessor names replace dashes with dots: libs.junit.jupiter.

concepts.name: Multi-project builds
concepts.summary: Split a build into subprojects, share settings with convention plugins, and let projects depend on each other.
concepts.why: Real codebases have many modules; structuring them well keeps builds fast and dependencies honest.
concepts.body:
A **multi-project build** has one `settings.gradle.kts` that includes several subprojects, each with its own `build.gradle.kts` in its folder:

```kotlin
rootProject.name = "shop"
include("core", "api", "app")
```

Subprojects are addressed by path: `:core`, `:services:billing` for nested folders. Run a task in one project with `./gradlew :api:test`; running `./gradlew test` from the root runs it in every project that has it.

Projects depend on each other with `implementation(project(":core"))`. Gradle then builds `core` first and uses its JAR (with compile avoidance when only internals changed). Never let projects depend on each other in a circle.

Sharing settings: the old `subprojects { }` / `allprojects { }` blocks in the top-level script are discouraged, because one project's script reaches into the others, which hides where settings come from and breaks newer speed features such as the configuration cache (Advanced). The recommended way is a **convention plugin**: a small plugin written as a build script, kept in the special `buildSrc` folder (`buildSrc/src/main/kotlin/acme.java-conventions.gradle.kts`) or in a separate helper build under `build-logic/`, that applies `java`, sets the toolchain, test settings and common dependencies. Each subproject then just writes `plugins { id("acme.java-conventions") }`.

A `gradle.properties` at the root holds shared properties such as `version` and JVM settings. `./gradlew projects` prints the project tree. A **composite build** (`includeBuild("../lib")`) pulls in a whole separate build, so you can use your local copy of a library's source code instead of its published version.
takeaways: include(...) in settings defines subprojects, addressed as :name
implementation(project(":core")) depends on a sibling
Share setup with convention plugins in buildSrc or build-logic, not subprojects { }
./gradlew :api:test runs a task in one project
pitfalls: Configuring subprojects from the root with subprojects { }, which breaks newer features like the configuration cache.

quiz.q: What is the recommended way to apply the same JDK toolchain and test setup to ten subprojects?
options: Copy the blocks into each build.gradle.kts
A shell script that edits the files
A convention plugin in buildSrc or build-logic applied by each subproject
quiz.explain: A convention plugin keeps the shared settings in one place, and each project opts in, so no script reaches into another project.

concepts.name: Incremental builds and the build cache
concepts.summary: Understand up-to-date checks, task inputs and outputs, the local and shared build cache, and the configuration cache.
concepts.why: Build speed depends on Gradle being able to skip work; misdeclared inputs make builds slow or wrong.
concepts.body:
Gradle avoids work at three levels.

**Up-to-date checks**: every task declares its **task inputs** (files, settings) and outputs. Before running a task, Gradle computes a **hash** of the inputs, a short fingerprint that changes whenever any input changes; if it and the outputs match the previous run, the task is skipped as `UP-TO-DATE`. Your own tasks must declare them, either with annotations (markers such as `@InputFile`, `@InputDirectory`, `@Input`, `@OutputDirectory`) on the properties of a task class, or with `inputs.files(...)` / `outputs.dir(...)` in scripts. Undeclared inputs give out-of-date results; undeclared outputs cause needless reruns.

**Build cache** (`org.gradle.caching=true` in `gradle.properties`): task outputs are stored under their input hash, so a task whose inputs were seen before, even on another branch or **another machine** through a shared remote cache (Develocity, Gradle's commercial service, or a plain HTTP cache server), is restored as `FROM-CACHE` instead of run. Compiling and tests can be cached; tasks must be **deterministic** (same inputs, same output) and declare all inputs. Mark your own task types `@CacheableTask`, and say how much file paths matter with `@PathSensitive`.

**Configuration cache** (`org.gradle.configuration-cache=true`): saves the result of the configuration phase to disk, so later builds skip running the scripts entirely. It requires that task actions don't reach back into the script's `project` object while running, and that values are passed with providers and `Property` types (see Writing plugins).

Inspect decisions with `--info` (reasons a task ran), `--scan` for a **build scan** (an online report of the whole build), and `./gradlew help --task x`. `--rerun-tasks` ignores up-to-date checks for debugging.
takeaways: Tasks skip when declared inputs and outputs are unchanged
The build cache restores outputs by input hash, from your machine or a shared server
The configuration cache skips the configuration phase
Undeclared inputs cause stale builds; declare everything
pitfalls: Reading a file or an environment variable (a setting passed in from outside the program) in a task without declaring it as an input, so changes are never picked up.

quiz.q: What does FROM-CACHE next to a task mean?
options: The task ran faster than usual
Its inputs were cached in memory
Its outputs were restored from the build cache without executing it
The task was skipped because it has no outputs
quiz.explain: A matching input hash was found in the build cache, so the stored outputs were reused.

concepts.name: Resolution, conflicts and BOMs
concepts.summary: Control transitive versions with platforms, strict versions, exclusions, substitutions and dependency locking.
concepts.why: Two libraries wanting different versions of a third, and transitive dependencies with security holes, are everyday problems; Gradle gives precise tools to fix them.
concepts.body:
Gradle works out the full **dependency graph**, every library and everything it needs, a step called resolution. Each library ends up with exactly one version per configuration. Gradle picks the **highest requested version** by default; this differs from Maven's nearest-wins rule. `./gradlew dependencyInsight --dependency <name> --configuration runtimeClasspath` shows every path and why a version won.

Tools to shape the result:

- **Platforms / BOMs**: `implementation(platform("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-dependencies:3.4.4"))` imports a BOM so all the libraries it lists get matching versions. `enforcedPlatform` wins even over higher requests.
- **Rich versions** say more than one number: `implementation("com.foo:bar") { version { strictly("[1.2, 2.0[") ; prefer("1.4") } }` means "from 1.2 up to but not including 2.0, ideally 1.4".
- **Constraints** adjust transitive versions without adding a direct dependency (e.g. to move to a version that fixes a known security hole).
- **Exclusions**: `implementation("x:y:1.0") { exclude(group = "commons-logging") }` leaves out an unwanted transitive dependency.
- **Substitution** in `configurations.all { resolutionStrategy.dependencySubstitution { ... } }` swaps one library for another, or for a project in your build.
- `resolutionStrategy.failOnVersionConflict()` makes conflicts explicit.
- **Capabilities** detect libraries that must not be used together (e.g. two competing logging back ends).

**Dependency locking** (`dependencyLocking { lockAllConfigurations() }` and `./gradlew dependencies --write-locks`) records the chosen versions in a **lock file**, `gradle.lockfile`, so builds stay the same even with version ranges. **Dependency verification** checks each downloaded file against a recorded **checksum** (a fingerprint of its bytes) and the publisher's signature, so tampered files are rejected.

Separate configurations (`compileClasspath`, `runtimeClasspath`, `testRuntimeClasspath`) may resolve to different versions, which is expected.
takeaways: Gradle resolves conflicts to the highest version unless told otherwise
platform(BOM) aligns versions across a family of modules
Constraints, strict versions and exclusions adjust transitives
Locking and verification make resolution reproducible and safe

quiz.q: Two transitive paths request library X at 1.2 and 1.5. Which does Gradle pick by default?
options: The one closest to the root, like Maven
quiz.explain: Gradle's default conflict resolution selects the highest requested version.

concepts.name: Publishing artifacts
concepts.summary: Publish libraries to Maven repositories with maven-publish, including the POM description, source files and signatures.
concepts.why: Sharing a library with other teams or the world means producing a correct Maven publication.
takeaways: maven-publish creates publications from the java component
api becomes Maven's compile scope, implementation becomes runtime
Source and Javadoc JARs, POM details and signatures are needed for Maven Central
Keep credentials in properties or environment variables

quiz.q: A consumer builds with Maven. How does your Gradle implementation dependency appear in the published POM?
quiz.explain: implementation dependencies are needed at run time but not for compiling against your API, so they map to runtime scope.

concepts.name: Writing plugins and lazy configuration
concepts.summary: Build reusable binary plugins with extensions, Property and Provider types, and typed tasks that follow Gradle's lazy configuration.
concepts.why: Convention and tooling plugins are how large organisations keep builds consistent; lazy configuration is what lets them work with Gradle's caches.
concepts.body:
A **binary plugin** is a plugin written as compiled code: a Kotlin or Java class implementing `Plugin<Project>`, usually kept in `build-logic` (a helper build included in yours) or in its own repository and published to a plugin repository. Its `apply(project)` method registers tasks, applies other plugins and creates an **extension** that users configure.

Gradle's modern API uses lazy configuration throughout:

- Use `Property<T>`, `ListProperty<T>`, `RegularFileProperty` and `DirectoryProperty` for extension and task fields, declared as `abstract val` so Gradle creates them for you.
- Wire values with providers instead of reading them eagerly: `task.outputDir.set(ext.outputDir)` links the two; the value is computed only when the task runs. Transform with `map { }` and `flatMap { }`; `project.provider { }` wraps arbitrary code.
- Register tasks with `tasks.register`, configure others with `tasks.named`, and avoid `project.afterEvaluate`.
- Never call `project` or `Project` services from `@TaskAction`; ask Gradle to hand you services (`ExecOperations`, `FileSystemOperations`, `ObjectFactory`) through `@Inject` instead, which is **dependency injection**: an object receives what it needs rather than fetching it. This keeps tasks compatible with the configuration cache.

Annotate task properties (`@Input`, `@InputFiles`, `@OutputDirectory`, `@Internal`, `@Nested`) so up-to-date checks and caching work; mark the task `@CacheableTask` when outputs are deterministic. Work inside a task can be split up to run in parallel with the **Worker API**.

Test plugins with **Gradle TestKit** (`GradleRunner`), which runs a real build in a temporary folder, and declare plugin ids in the `gradlePlugin { plugins { } }` block of the `java-gradle-plugin` so they can be applied by id. Publish with the `com.gradle.plugin-publish` plugin.
takeaways: A plugin class registers tasks and creates an extension in apply()
Use Property/Provider types and map/flatMap for lazy wiring
Annotate task inputs/outputs; inject services instead of using Project in actions
Test with TestKit's GradleRunner
pitfalls: Reading extension values eagerly in apply(), before the user's build script has set them.

quiz.q: Why wire task.message.set(ext.message) instead of task.message.set(ext.message.get()) inside apply()?
options: At apply time the user hasn't configured the extension yet; the provider link defers reading until execution
quiz.explain: Plugins are applied before the configuring block runs, so eager get() would read the default or fail; providers resolve lazily.

concepts.name: Build performance tuning
concepts.summary: Profile builds with scans and --profile, tune daemon memory, parallelism, configuration cache and remote caching.
concepts.why: Slow builds cost teams hours a day; most slowness has a diagnosable cause.
concepts.body:
Measure first. `./gradlew build --scan` publishes a build scan (on Develocity) with a timeline of tasks, configuration time, cache hits and dependency downloads; `--profile` writes a local HTML report to `build/reports/profile`. Look for: long configuration phase, tasks that are never up-to-date, tests dominating, and serial execution.

Settings in `gradle.properties` (project or `~/.gradle`):

- `org.gradle.parallel=true` runs tasks of independent subprojects at the same time; `org.gradle.workers.max` caps how many run at once.
- `org.gradle.caching=true` enables the build cache; add a remote cache so CI and developers share outputs.
- `org.gradle.configuration-cache=true` eliminates configuration time on repeated builds.
- `org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx4g -XX:+UseParallelGC` sets the daemon's memory (its **heap**, here 4 GB) and how it frees memory. Too little shows up as long pauses while the **garbage collector** clears space; too much leaves too little for compilers and test JVMs.
- `org.gradle.vfs.watch=true` (on by default) lets the daemon watch the project's files for changes, so it needn't re-check them all at the start of each build.

Structural fixes often matter more: split large modules so compile avoidance and caching bite, keep configuration-phase code cheap (no reading files or network calls), use `tasks.register` not `tasks.create`, prefer `implementation` over `api` so one change doesn't force many projects to recompile, and run slow integration tests in their own task.

For tests, `maxParallelForks`, `forkEvery` and JUnit 5's parallel execution help. Keep the daemon alive in CI (or use `--no-daemon` with a persistent cache); starting fresh JVMs and downloading dependencies dominate CI time, so cache `~/.gradle/caches` and `~/.gradle/wrapper`.

Upgrading Gradle, the JDK and plugins regularly brings free performance work.
takeaways: Measure with --scan or --profile before changing anything
parallel, caching and configuration cache are the big three switches
Size the daemon JVM sensibly and cache ~/.gradle in CI
Modularize and keep configuration cheap for structural wins
pitfalls: Giving the daemon a huge heap and wondering why test JVMs and the operating system run short of memory and slow to a crawl.

quiz.q: A build scan shows every compileJava task running on every build despite no code changes. What's the likely cause?
options: A task input that changes each build (timestamp, undeclared file) invalidates up-to-date checks
quiz.explain: An input that changes every time, or one Gradle doesn't know about, defeats up-to-date checks, so tasks always rerun.

concepts.name: Variants, attributes and capabilities
concepts.summary: Understand how Gradle picks the right variant of a library by its attributes (JAR or classes, JVM version, optional features), and how to debug it.
concepts.why: Cryptic 'no matching variant' errors and multi-flavor Android or multiplatform libraries all come down to this model.
concepts.body:
Gradle dependencies are not just coordinates: each library offers several **variants**, different sets of files for different uses (for a Java library: `apiElements`, `runtimeElements`, `sourcesElements`, `javadocElements`). A dependency configuration that uses the library picks one by matching **variant attributes**, labels describing what each variant is for.

Standard attributes include `org.gradle.usage` (`java-api` vs `java-runtime`), `org.gradle.category` (`library`, `platform`, `documentation`), `org.gradle.libraryelements` (`jar`, `classes`, `resources`), `org.gradle.jvm.version` (the lowest JVM version it runs on) and, for Kotlin Multiplatform (Kotlin for several platforms at once) and Android, platform and build-type attributes. `compileClasspath` asks for `java-api` + `classes` when possible, which is why compiling can use the compiled class folders of other projects in the build without packing them into JARs first.

The rules are published in Gradle Module Metadata (`.module` files) next to POMs, so variant selection also works for published libraries. For a library with only a Maven POM, Gradle makes up two variants (compile and runtime).

Common errors and fixes:

- "No matching variant" usually means the producer targets a newer JVM (`org.gradle.jvm.version=21`) than the consumer's toolchain, or an Android/KMP library lacks a variant for your platform. Align toolchains or add the missing target.
- Ambiguity errors appear when two variants match equally well; add a rule that says which to prefer, or ask for a more specific attribute.

**Capabilities** declare what a variant provides; two modules providing the same capability conflict (such as two logging back ends, `slf4j-simple` and `logback-classic`). **Feature variants** (`java { registerFeature("mongo") { usingSourceSet(...) } }`) publish optional features with their own dependencies, which users request with `requireCapabilities`. (A **source set** is a group of source files compiled together, such as `main` or `test`.)

Debug with `./gradlew outgoingVariants` (what a project offers) and `./gradlew resolvableConfigurations` (what it asks for), and `dependencyInsight`, which prints the selected variant and attributes.
takeaways: Libraries offer variants; configurations pick one by matching attributes
usage, category, libraryelements and jvm.version are the key attributes
'No matching variant' is usually a JVM target or platform mismatch
outgoingVariants and resolvableConfigurations show both sides

quiz.q: Your library compiled with a JDK 21 toolchain is consumed by a project on JDK 17. What happens?
options: It works; Gradle downgrades the bytecode
Resolution fails: no variant matches org.gradle.jvm.version 17 (or lower)
Gradle silently uses the runtime variant
quiz.explain: The producer's variants carry jvm.version=21, which a JDK 17 consumer cannot accept, so variant matching fails.
